policy.counterexampleRule: A counterexample defeats or conditions an over-broad design assumption; it does not invert into a universal anti-pattern.
policy.transferRule: Every record must expose context, a failure signal, revision/salvage, transfer boundary, false universalizations, and a cheap discriminator.

counterexamples.assumption: A guided campaign can represent a sandbox core by approximating freeplay while adding quests, bounded areas and staged progression.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The playable campaign introduced unexpected problems and was judged less fun than freeplay despite being designed to represent it.
counterexamples.context: Factorio's core value depended heavily on self-directed freeplay; the campaign added bounded map progression, short-term quests and environmental gates while trying to remain representative.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Wube cancelled the campaign for 1.0 and refocused on the core game, while keeping separate scenarios as a possible form of side content.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: This conditions campaigns that claim to demonstrate an open sandbox core; it does not argue against authored campaigns with a different target experience.
falseUniversalizations: Guidance necessarily damages sandbox games.
Campaigns are inferior to freeplay.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Compare one identical sandbox slice under self-authored goals and quest-gated progression; enumerate which strategic choices disappear or become externally selected.

counterexamples.assumption: If a tutorial/demo broadens appeal and receives strong positive newcomer feedback, it is therefore a good product representation.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The NPE achieved many local onboarding/appeal goals yet the team still removed it because it did not represent the intended core experience well enough.
counterexamples.context: The tutorial doubled as a demo and was designed to expose more mid-game content; later campaign cancellation also changed what the demo was supposed to lead into.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Wube restored an older tutorial/demo direction aligned more closely with the core game rather than optimizing only the locally successful NPE.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: This attacks proxy substitution between onboarding success and product fidelity, not the value of newcomer feedback itself.
falseUniversalizations: Positive onboarding feedback proves the demo is representative.
Internal creative vision should override player evidence.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Before rating a demo, compare its dominant goals, constraints and player-authored decisions with the first sustained core-product loop.

counterexamples.assumption: If an invalid state is almost never desired, the system should make that state globally impossible.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Strict fluid-mixing prevention accumulated edge-case complexity for roughly a year and a half without becoming graceful across the existing game.
counterexamples.context: The invariant was introduced after a large legacy fluid/construction system already existed, so exhaustive prevention had to cover many merge/build operations.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Wube simplified prevention to the common manual-building case and added a fast flush/recovery mechanism for harder cases.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Recovery is not appropriate where entering the invalid state has unacceptable irreversible consequences.
falseUniversalizations: Recovery is always cheaper than prevention.
Invalid states should always be impossible by construction.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Implement exhaustive prevention and common-case prevention plus recovery for one bounded subsystem; compare branch count, edge cases and recovery steps.

counterexamples.assumption: Additional tabs and duplicate access points necessarily improve organization and discoverability.
counterexamples.failureSignal: A Character tab became filler/duplication and nested crafting tabs disrupted a frequently repeated workflow.
counterexamples.context: The same information/actions were already visible elsewhere, and crafting category switching was a high-frequency interaction.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The duplicate Character tab was removed and the flatter GUI became the default.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Distinct task domains or low-frequency workflows can still benefit from tabs and alternate entry points.
falseUniversalizations: Flat UI is always better than tabs.
More discoverable entry points are always beneficial.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: For the exact frequent task, count equivalent-control mappings and mode switches under nested/duplicated versus single-location layouts.

counterexamples.assumption: A visually impressive individual asset will remain a good design when deployed in the real play context.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The Beacon redesign attracted too much attention once considered at factory density and zoom, prompting another redesign.
counterexamples.context: Beacons can appear in large repeated groups while serving a supporting rather than primary-attention function.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The redesign reduced salience while preserving enough close-up visual explanation of function.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Rare critical objects may intentionally require high salience; density and camera distance are part of the design condition.
falseUniversalizations: Visually impressive assets are better assets.
Supporting objects should always be visually quiet.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Evaluate the same asset at isolated, typical-density and worst-case-density views before polishing it in isolation.

counterexamples.assumption: A valuable convenience/market system can be added beside the core loop without changing what efficient players optimize for.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Blizzard concluded that the Auction House, despite real benefits and use, undermined the core kill-monsters-for-loot loop.
counterexamples.context: A global efficient market competed directly with the game's item-acquisition reward path under the launch itemization/drop economy.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The Auction House was removed while Loot 2.0, itemization and rewards were redesigned around finding exciting items through play.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Trading does not necessarily displace core play when its efficiency, scarcity and reward relationship are configured differently.
falseUniversalizations: Player trading is bad for loot games.
Useful secondary systems cannot damage a core loop.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Model the expected advancement frontier for core activity versus the secondary system and find where optimal behavior switches away from the intended loop.

counterexamples.assumption: More preproduction inventory only increases later design options because unused concepts are cheap to ignore.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Some of the large character inventory became filler that designers were reluctant to cut after story/mission purposes changed.
counterexamples.context: The team had created more than 200 character concepts before all downstream roles were known.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The useful lesson is not to avoid broad ideation but to make revalidation/deletion cheap as the design changes.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Large inventories remain valuable when they carry no implicit survival rights and can be discarded without sunk-cost pressure.
falseUniversalizations: Preproduction should be minimized.
More concepts always expand optionality at no cost.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Give each preproduction item an expiry/revalidation point; compare retained items under default-keep versus default-delete policies.

counterexamples.assumption: Creative constraints necessarily shrink the design search space and therefore reduce creativity.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Double Fine's postmortem describes empathy as a focus that expanded design possibility rather than merely removing options.
counterexamples.context: The constraint changed how a narrative platformer could represent minds, characters and conflict while modernizing a sequel.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Treat some constraints as search operators that generate new relations/questions, not only filters that reject candidates.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: A vague or irrelevant constraint can still shrink search without producing useful new structure.
falseUniversalizations: Fewer constraints always produce more creativity.
Strong values automatically improve creative work.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Generate candidate mechanisms with and without one explicit constraint and compare structural diversity/new relationships, not subjective quality scores.

counterexamples.assumption: More mechanics/content naturally improve a systemic strategy game by creating more variety.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The project accumulated years of cut content and redesign while converging on a small state space with high interaction density.
counterexamples.context: The final design depends on legible tactical consequences and combinatorial interaction inside a very compact board/state space.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Cutting and constraint pruning can increase interaction density when extra content adds states without adding meaningful decisions.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Content breadth can still be valuable where discovery, collection or long-horizon variety is the target.
falseUniversalizations: Small games are more systemic.
More content reduces strategic depth.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Remove one candidate content family and enumerate lost decision distinctions versus removed state/teaching burden.

counterexamples.assumption: Features commonly considered necessary for a genre/product must be implemented before the unique value can work.
counterexamples.failureSignal: RimWorld shipped while omitting features that might normally be considered critical, because the team prioritized features serving its story-generator value.
counterexamples.context: A tiny team framed the product around systemic story generation rather than completeness against a conventional checklist.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Require a candidate feature to name the relationship/value it serves instead of inheriting mandatory status from genre convention.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Some features are real prerequisites due to platform, accessibility, safety or exact product contracts.
falseUniversalizations: Genre conventions are optional by default.
Missing features create differentiation.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Delete one assumed-required feature in a cheap prototype and test whether the claimed unique interaction remains reachable and legible.

counterexamples.assumption: Once an idea reaches prototype form, retaining and polishing it is usually cheaper than abandoning it.
counterexamples.failureSignal: FTL's developers describe frequent alteration/abandonment as normal while searching for a target feeling rather than preserving prototypes.
counterexamples.context: The project prioritized an experiential target above genre or mechanic precommitment and kept prototype attachment deliberately low.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Use prototype survival as an evidence question rather than a reward for implementation effort already spent.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Late-stage production assets carry different replacement cost than throwaway search prototypes.
falseUniversalizations: Prototypes should be disposable at every production stage.
Keeping a prototype is evidence that it is good.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Before polishing, require each prototype to beat a deliberately different alternative on the exact target relationship or return to the search pool.

counterexamples.assumption: If community secret hunting is engaging, making the hidden search space larger or less bounded only creates more discovery value.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The developer account explicitly notes that community puzzle search can become unhealthy over-search and therefore needs boundaries.
counterexamples.context: Secrets and collective discovery are part of the game's identity, which makes over-search a risk produced by the same mechanism that creates value.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Bound or signal the search space so mystery can persist without implying endless undiscovered obligations.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: The harm boundary depends on community behavior, secret signaling and the cost of exhaustive search.
falseUniversalizations: More hidden content always improves mystery games.
Community collaboration makes unbounded search safe.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: For one secret system, vary whether exhausted regions can be inferred; compare the mechanically implied search space before any engagement claim.

counterexamples.assumption: Reducing interface opacity and friction is always aligned with improving a game.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Cultist Simulator deliberately retained unusual/divisive interface and learning-through-discovery choices as part of its niche identity.
counterexamples.context: Discovering the system itself was part of the intended experience, making some uncertainty content rather than only usability debt.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Separate causal ambiguity needed for discovery from accidental friction that blocks intended reasoning.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Opacity becomes harder to justify when errors are irreversible or the hidden relation is not itself meaningful content.
falseUniversalizations: Usability best practices should be ignored for mysterious games.
Friction creates identity.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Hide one relation while keeping probing reversible, then separately add pure interaction friction; compare whether either changes the intended inference structure.

counterexamples.assumption: More procedural variation is intrinsically better because replayable content should approach infinity.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Firaxis treated procedural level generation as a bounded tradeoff with authored tactical requirements and production cost rather than pursuing unlimited variation.
counterexamples.context: Generated layouts still had to support specific tactical geometry, encounter requirements and production constraints.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Generate only dimensions whose variation adds value while explicitly constraining properties that must remain tactically valid.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Some games make surprise or generative novelty itself the primary target and may tolerate a wider validity envelope.
falseUniversalizations: Procedural generation should maximize unique outputs.
Authored content is always more reliable than procedural content.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Name one invariant tactical property and one desired variable dimension; generate only the latter and count rejected outputs that violate the former.

counterexamples.assumption: Once a design is desirable in principle, production organization and tooling are downstream implementation concerns.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Larian's postmortems repeatedly connect reactivity scale and cinematic/content ambition to toolchain, team and organizational changes.
counterexamples.context: Highly reactive branching content multiplies cross-discipline state, authoring and production dependencies.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Treat throughput/tool/team topology as part of the feasible design space when the design creates combinatorial authoring obligations.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Small bounded prototypes can ignore organization temporarily when they are not making production feasibility claims.
falseUniversalizations: Production constraints should shape all early ideation.
Good tools make arbitrarily complex reactive content feasible.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: For one reactive feature, enumerate authoring, cinematic, QA and state combinations before implementation; test whether a thin tool/representation collapses the dominant burden.

counterexamples.assumption: Large changes in scope, perspective or visual style necessarily destroy a project's identity and therefore should be resisted.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Saturnalia's six-year development survived radical changes across those dimensions while retaining enough identity to continue toward the shipped work.
counterexamples.context: The project experienced financing pressure and long development, so survival responses and design discoveries were intertwined.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Identify the actual identity-bearing invariant instead of preserving every current form around it.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: The source does not show that arbitrary radical change is cheap or safe; some transformations can still erase the target experience.
falseUniversalizations: Pivoting destroys project identity.
A strong identity makes large pivots safe.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Name one identity-bearing relationship and mutate scope, camera or representation separately; test whether the relationship still exists mechanically.

counterexamples.assumption: If a predecessor already feels complete, a sequel must either repeat it or violate its identity.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Valve's sequel process treats completeness as a design problem to solve, not proof that the possibility space is closed.
counterexamples.context: Portal already had a very compact, recognizable core verb and authored puzzle identity.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Preserve an identity-bearing core while searching for new elements/relationships that multiply the possibility space around it.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: A sequel still needs a meaningful new search direction; preserving a core alone does not justify expansion.
falseUniversalizations: Complete games should not have sequels.
Sequels must replace the old core to be novel.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Freeze one identity-bearing verb and prototype one new relation around it; compare possibility growth with a simple content-only extension.

counterexamples.assumption: Once a design has been rejected as too complex, that verdict should remain stable unless the original analysis was wrong.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Factorio later revisited mixed-load logistics after system capability and observed player planning changed the surrounding conditions.
counterexamples.context: The earlier complexity judgement was made against a different system and planning environment than the later one.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Attach rejection to its conditions and reopen when those conditions materially change rather than treating the decision as eternal law.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Reopening still requires a changed premise; novelty alone is not evidence that an old rejection expired.
falseUniversalizations: Old rejected ideas deserve periodic revival by default.
A validated rejection is permanent design law.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Store the exact premise behind a rejection and rerun its cheapest falsifier only when that premise changes.

counterexamples.assumption: If individual new content additions each look useful during incremental development, the full product benefits from continuing to add them.
counterexamples.failureSignal: A start-to-finish playthrough exposed cumulative size/phase density that local feature work had not made salient.
counterexamples.context: Factorio's long progression means local additions accumulate across many phases before the whole-run burden becomes visible.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The team shifted attention toward optimization and contextual teaching rather than simply increasing vanilla content.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Short products or independently consumable content may not accumulate the same whole-run saturation.
falseUniversalizations: Full playthroughs are always superior to focused feature tests.
More content eventually makes every game worse.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Run the smallest end-to-end traversal that preserves all progression phases and record cumulative transitions/dead zones before deciding on another content family.

counterexamples.assumption: A long-term vision that originally motivated the team should keep receiving resources until it is fulfilled, especially after years of investment.
counterexamples.failureSignal: The director later described continued pursuit of the old crawl-walk-run PvE/MMO strategy as not working, with scope growth, cohesion problems and repeated resource diversion from the successful live game.
counterexamples.context: The vision originated in cancelled Project Titan and persisted after Overwatch became a runaway hit; Hero Missions then accumulated years of work and public expectation.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Hero Missions were cut, the future vision was updated, and the team retained other story/co-op work rather than preserving the original plan wholesale.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: This attacks premise-free persistence, not long-range vision itself; a future bet can remain valid when current evidence and opportunity cost still support it.
falseUniversalizations: Old visions should be discarded after launch success.
Live products should never fund ambitious parallel bets.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Re-state the original vision’s premises using current product evidence and run a bounded end-to-end slice under an explicit resource envelope before extending sunk investment.

counterexamples.assumption: If the gameplay is becoming refined, satisfying and directionally strong, the project should proceed to full production.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Naughty Dog cancelled despite reporting improving gameplay because years of post-launch support would consume studio-wide resources and change what kind of studio it was.
counterexamples.context: The project was a large live-service extension inside a studio that also wanted to preserve multiple ambitious single-player projects.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The project was stopped while its technology and development learning were explicitly retained for future work.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: A different studio/team topology or bounded support model could make the same gameplay feasible.
falseUniversalizations: Good gameplay is irrelevant if operations are expensive.
Live-service projects are incompatible with narrative studios.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Before full production, build the minimum credible multi-year staffing/content/ops graph and test whether protected parallel products still fit without assuming future hiring solves the gap.

counterexamples.assumption: If a reboot fixes most game-side complaints and reaches its gameplay goals, continued development becomes justified.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Valve reported reasonable satisfaction with most game-side goals but still stopped development because active player numbers were insufficient.
counterexamples.context: The reboot followed a polarizing initial release, dramatic population decline, a changed economy and a limited/gradual beta ramp.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Both versions were preserved as free products rather than continuing service development or deleting the work.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Low current population can be caused by access, reputation or market factors; it is not a direct gameplay-quality measure.
falseUniversalizations: Gameplay improvements cannot rescue a failed launch.
A good redesign will naturally rebuild a sustainable audience.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Track game-side acceptance separately from acquisition, activation, retention and concurrency; require the proposed reboot to name which lane is the actual bottleneck.

referenceGames: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn
counterexamples.assumption: Once an online game has shipped, incremental repair is necessarily safer or more realistic than product-level replacement.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Square Enix chose a full relaunch after the unsuccessful 2010 release and explicitly treated relaunch importance and initial failure causes as the core postmortem problem.
counterexamples.context: A major branded MMORPG had live/business obligations but also foundation-level product problems serious enough to motivate a replacement built in roughly two years and nine months.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The response was a new product-level implementation under an explicit business commitment rather than treating the original shipped form as immutable.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Relaunch is unusually expensive and brand/resource dependent; local repair remains preferable when failure dependencies are bounded.
falseUniversalizations: Failed live games should be relaunched instead of patched.
Shipping makes foundational replacement impossible.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Map central failure claims to subsystem dependency closure and compare a bounded repair path against one clean replacement slice before choosing either.

counterexamples.assumption: Once most world, features and playable content exist, large narrative changes are too late and polishing is the rational default.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Unknown Worlds said the experience was broadly playable but not working in harmony, particularly the living story, and committed to a new story.
counterexamples.context: World substrate and many characters/features were already present in Early Access; the rewrite preserved selected validated pieces rather than resetting everything.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The story layer was rewritten while world, creatures and valued characters were retained and reconnected.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: A late rewrite only makes sense when the failing relationship is central enough and salvage boundaries are identifiable.
falseUniversalizations: Late projects should accept incoherent design to avoid rewrite cost.
Near-complete builds should be freely rewritten when something feels off.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Graph the failing experience relationship onto existing assets; if repair touches many high-centrality edges, compare selective rewrite against local polish before producing more content.

counterexamples.assumption: A detailed long-horizon roadmap is merely informational until someone explicitly marks its items committed.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Unknown Worlds described its roadmap as creating pressure to deliver scheduled items regardless of importance, obscuring the whole game and contributing to recurring crunch.
counterexamples.context: An Early Access team publicly planned many small and large features across frequent releases despite acknowledged uncertainty.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The process shifted toward release columns containing only highlighted/ready work while the majority of the team focused on big-picture game needs.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Roadmaps can remain useful when hypothesis/commitment status, expiry and deletion semantics are explicit.
falseUniversalizations: Roadmaps inherently cause crunch.
Only short-term planning preserves creativity.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Attach status and expiry to roadmap items; on the next cycle, attempt to delete or defer hypotheses and observe whether process/social mechanics treat them as hidden commitments.

counterexamples.assumption: A healthy live service must preserve its promised content cadence even while technical debt and deployment risk accumulate.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Ubisoft replaced a planned season with Operation Health, delayed content, reduced annual map output and prioritized deployment/rollback/bug infrastructure.
counterexamples.context: The game already had an active community and recurring technical problems; the intervention explicitly traded near-term content throughput for platform health.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The team introduced staged rollout and fast rollback while rescheduling rather than abandoning the content roadmap wholesale.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Content pauses are not justified when substrate health is not the actual bottleneck or when remediation goals are unbounded.
falseUniversalizations: Live games should pause content whenever technical debt exists.
Breaking release cadence necessarily harms a live service more than technical debt.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Quantify recurring incident severity and release-induced regressions, then trial staged rollout plus rollback on one release before sacrificing a full content cycle.

counterexamples.assumption: Foundational rules in a shipped live game become effectively immutable because too much content and balance depend on them.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Bungie shipped a fundamental weapon-slot reversal and rebuilt ammo distribution/damage tuning around it in Forsaken.
counterexamples.context: The old model had a large installed inventory and both PvE/PvP balance dependencies; migration was performed as part of an expansion-scale change.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Existing weapons were remapped into the new Kinetic/Energy/Primary/Special foundation rather than preserving old taxonomy for compatibility alone.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Foundation reversal has high migration and tuning cost and should target a real structural bottleneck, not ordinary balance dissatisfaction.
falseUniversalizations: Live-game foundations should be rewritten whenever players dislike the meta.
Shipped foundational rules cannot be replaced safely.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Prototype target loadout choices under both old and revised taxonomies, then enumerate migration/tuning closure before declaring the foundation untouchable or disposable.

counterexamples.assumption: Multiplayer can be deferred until the single-player game is mature because it is an optional social feature.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Unknown Worlds concluded that adding multiplayer late would affect nearly everything and require many months/years or near-restart-scale work.
counterexamples.context: The original concept considered co-op, but multiplayer was skipped during early development to ship sooner; the architecture then matured around single-player assumptions.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The original game committed to single-player while leaving multiplayer as a possibility for a future/new game built around it.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: This applies when multiplayer changes authority, persistence, simulation or interaction ownership; network-ready architectures can have a different cost profile.
falseUniversalizations: Multiplayer should always be designed from day one.
Single-player architecture is simpler and therefore better.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Build one co-op vertical slice spanning state authority, save/load, interaction conflict and reconnect before treating multiplayer as a deferrable checkbox.

counterexamples.assumption: More freedom in team composition necessarily increases player agency without meaningful systemic cost.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Open role choice pushed composition negotiation into a short social window and Blizzard cited pressure, disappointment and hostility as recurring problems.
counterexamples.context: Players had heterogeneous role preferences but team performance strongly depended on role coverage.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Role Queue moved role commitment into matchmaking and guaranteed a composition structure, trading some composition freedom for reduced negotiation burden.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Premade groups or games with weak role dependencies may preserve open selection without the same social cost.
falseUniversalizations: Fixed roles create healthier social play by default.
Open composition systems inevitably become toxic.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Count forced concessions, unresolved role gaps and negotiation actions under free selection versus precommitted-role matchmaking before evaluating subjective preference.

counterexamples.assumption: Once a fixed role structure solves composition and social problems, keeping that structure is mostly a balance problem rather than a population-flow problem.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Fixed 2-2-2 queues were throughput-limited by tank supply; Blizzard later reported 1-2-2 matched observed demand better and reduced waits.
counterexamples.context: Role popularity was persistently uneven, making the least-popular required role a matchmaking bottleneck.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Team composition rules were reconsidered alongside 5v5 rather than treating the earlier social fix as costless infrastructure.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: The bottleneck disappears when role arrival rates match required ratios or roles are substitutable.
falseUniversalizations: Role Queue was a mistake.
Team size should be chosen to match popularity alone.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Use measured role arrival rates to model match throughput under candidate team ratios before locking composition constraints.

counterexamples.assumption: A broad low-severity reward penalty is a safe first-line deterrent because it discourages harmful behavior without strongly punishing edge cases.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Blizzard said the XP penalty was insufficient for deliberate leavers while still negatively affecting unintentional leavers.
counterexamples.context: Leaving can arise from both deliberate disruption and incidental disconnect/life events, but the initial penalty did not distinguish intent well.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The team moved toward escalating queue suspensions tied to repeated leaving patterns.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Different telemetry, reward value or behavior distributions can make softer penalties effective.
falseUniversalizations: Harsh penalties are better deterrents.
Behavior systems should infer player intent directly.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Segment repeat-pattern and isolated leaving cohorts, then compare expected penalty salience and false-positive exposure before changing severity.

counterexamples.assumption: Adding a scarce currency to upgrades creates meaningful progression decisions because players must choose when to spend it.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Bungie concluded Unstable Cores were broadly restrictive but did not drive interesting buildcraft decisions, then chose deprecation.
counterexamples.context: The currency gated infusion for both campaign progression and endgame experimentation across many items.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Infusion costs were moved back to established currencies rather than preserving the new resource for sunk-design reasons.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Scarcity remains valuable when it creates distinct opportunity costs among meaningful alternatives.
falseUniversalizations: Upgrade currencies are bad design.
Removing friction always improves experimentation.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Enumerate which branches of player strategy change because of the currency; if it only delays all branches similarly, test deletion or replacement.

counterexamples.assumption: A mature universal currency should be retained because compatibility and player familiarity make it cheaper than economy migration.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Legendary Shards were progressively removed from vendor/crafting costs and ultimately phased out despite their long history and broad integration.
counterexamples.context: Veteran balances, inflation and newer engram/resource systems had changed the economy around the currency.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Costs migrated toward more specific currencies/resources and the old currency was sunset in stages.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: A universal currency with a coherent unique role may still reduce complexity rather than add baggage.
falseUniversalizations: Old currencies should eventually be removed.
More specialized currencies always produce better economies.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Map every source/spend edge and the unique decision it creates; treat compatibility-only edges with no distinct decision as migration candidates, not automatic deletions.

counterexamples.assumption: More reusable/deduplicated procedural-generation abstractions are necessarily better because they reduce repeated computation and authoring duplication.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Cross-procedure deduplication created dependency and compile/runtime complexity; Wube removed the procedure abstraction and reported better performance in measured cases.
counterexamples.context: Noise programs were compiled for distinct generation outputs and actual reuse did not justify dependency machinery.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: The generator moved to simpler multi-output programs with inlining and automatic lifetime reuse.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Reusable subgraphs can still win when reuse is substantial or authoring correctness dominates performance.
falseUniversalizations: Flattened procedural graphs are faster by default.
Abstraction is harmful in generation systems.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Compare a representative graph as reusable procedures and a flattened multi-output form across compile time, runtime, authoring duplication and dependency complexity.

counterexamples.assumption: Independent procedural subsystems can evolve separately as long as each works locally; integration can be handled with settings and adapters.
counterexamples.failureSignal: Separate terrain and resource/autoplace systems made desired placement behavior difficult to express, produced pathological outputs and motivated a large unification refactor.
counterexamples.context: Cross-cutting requirements such as predictable starting resources depended on several procedural dimensions that lived in incompatible representations.
counterexamples.revisionOrSalvage: Legacy specifications were compiled into a common expression-tree representation while preserving compatibility at the boundary.
counterexamples.transferBoundary: Small generators with few cross-system constraints may not benefit from unification.
falseUniversalizations: All procedural systems should share one representation.
Generator bugs imply the architecture needs a rewrite.
counterexamples.cheapDiscriminator: Express one important cross-system invariant in the current architecture and count special cases/adapters versus a shared intermediate representation before rewriting.
